newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMI report casts doubt on broad EMU start - analysts.
newsitem.headline: EMI report casts doubt on broad EMU start - analysts.

text.p: The prospects for a broad starting line-up for European economic and monetary union (EMU) were dimmed by the European Monetary Institute's annual report on Tuesday, economists said.

But with a growing realisation that politics, not economics, will wield more clout when the "ins" and "outs" are picked in 1998, financial markets, and individual governments, should not be unduly perturbed.

While EMI criticism of budgetary positions, levelled across the spectrum of European Union nations, will tweak nerves in the so-called Club Med countries more than others, the core countries of France and Germany did not emerge from the 1996 annual report with a clean sheet either.
"If monetary union were left purely down to the EMI, then you could say this report is bad news for the broad EMU story," said Darren Williams, European economist at UBS in London.
"But the EMI is only one of the two bodies which will advise on suitable EMU candidates, and we all suspect that the European Commission will have a dominant role in that."

The EMI, the embryo of the European Central Bank, lashed out at one-off tricks reducing deficit to growth ratios, saying they "cannot be regarded as contributing to sustainability". It also said heavy reliance on higher revenues rather than spending cuts to rein deficits in was "a ground for concern".

The Maastricht Treaty, which sets out the entry criteria and timetable for the European single currency, says government deficits should be reduced to at most three percent of gross domestic product before countries can join the euro.
"On the fiscal side, the situation remains far from satisfactory in many countries," the institute's president, Alexandre Lamfalussy, said in a foreword to the report.
Analysts said the main thrust of the report was to serve as a reminder that sustainable convergence is of primary importance and that entry for all the EMU-hopefuls is not a foregone conclusion.

"This is good news for Germany. We think that Germany will miss the deficit target by 0.4 percent. But it is good news nevertheless because Germany has had quite a solid underlying fiscal performance," said Joerg Kraemer, economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt.
The sharpest words, analysts said, were directed at the likes of Portugal, Italy, Denmark and Spain, who have no such comparable history of fiscal restraint.
"EMU membership for Club Med countries is not yet a done deal -- that is clear," said one.
At the same time, Germany was not exempt from the scolding.

"It is a criticism of almost every country in Europe, not just in terms of one-off accounting measures but also in terms of reliance on such things as higher revenue as opposed to government spending cuts," said Williams.

On monetary policy and inflation, too, analysts said the EMI's tone was concerned, with some viewing the comments as a veiled warning to the Bundesbank, which has kept German interest rates steady at historically low levels since August.

"Our economic research suggests that the Bundesbank should have started to hike interest rates in the Autumn of last year. And if monetary policy is too relaxed for too long, this may build up inflationary pressure which may become a problem in 1999. This is the fear of the EMI. They are worried that the European Central Bank will have a problem at the very beginning of its life," said Kraemer.
The EMI, which will be superseded by the ECB early in 1998, urged vigilance on price stability, saying that upward risks to EU inflation remained.

"The stance adopted in the period ahead will be particularly important in that it will increasingly affect inflation in 1999 and thereafter, and hence price expectations for the euro area," the report said.
But other analysts said the EMI was merely flexing its muscles, keen to pave a credible path for its successor.

"The EMI -- and the ECB as it will soon become -- realises that it needs to establish its inflation credentials very, very early in the day," said Williams. "I think that was probably their main aim here."
